## Confirmed: the duplication is real

`crimes scan --format json` returns 5 findings, three of which are the duplication story:

| id | charge | files | confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `crime_00002` | Near-Duplicate Block | `sanitize-a.ts:10-36`, `sanitize-b.ts:9-35`, `sanitize-c.ts:9-35` | 0.85 |
| `crime_00001` | Exact Duplicate Block | `telemetry-a.ts:6-19`, `telemetry-b.ts:6-19` | 0.95 |
| `crime_00003` | Duplicated Role/Status/Plan Check | `policy.ts` + all three `sanitize-*.ts` | 0.70 |

I read the three files to check the detector wasn't over-reporting. It isn't — and it's actually *understating* the case. The three sanitise bodies are **token-identical apart from identifier names**:

- `sanitizeUserInput(raw)` / `working` (a)
- `sanitizeText(input)` / `cleaned` (b)
- `cleanMessage(value)` / `normalised` (c)

Same trim, same `[\x00-\x1f]` strip (written as raw control bytes in source — see below), same `\s+`→space collapse, same 1000-char truncation, same `<`/`>` prefix reject, same `\\x` reject, same `[!?]{3,}` > 5 reject, same 0.9-upper-ratio-over-30-chars lowercasing. No behavioural difference to preserve. `near_duplicate` rather than `exact_duplicate` is purely the renaming.

**The one place the copies genuinely diverge is the admin guard**, and this is the trap:

```ts
assertAdminA(role) → role === "admin"          // a
assertAdminB(role) → role === "admin" || role === "owner"   // b — wider
assertAdminC(role) → role !== "admin"          // c — INVERTED
```

These are three different predicates wearing near-identical names. `assertAdminC` returns `true` for non-admins. Any refactor that "consolidates the admin checks" by picking one implementation silently flips authorisation for whoever calls `assertAdminC`. That's the `agent_risk` 0.50 on `crime_00003` earning its keep — and it's why this finding gets `effort: medium` while the sanitiser gets `small`.

## Proposed refactor

**Three independent moves, in this order** (each is separately revertible):

**1. Extract the sanitiser** — `src/sanitize.ts` holds one implementation. The three old files become thin re-export shims so callers don't break in the same commit. Since the bodies are identical, this is a pure behaviour-preserving move; the magic numbers become named options rather than staying inline.

**2. Extract telemetry** — `src/telemetry.ts` holds one `recordSanitiseEvent`. While the block is being touched anyway, take the `direct_date` findings (`crime_00004`/`crime_00005`, `Date.now()` at line 16 of both copies) with it by accepting an injected clock. Fixing it once post-consolidation is the cheap moment; fixing it twice pre-consolidation is not.

**3. Centralise the policy check — carefully.** Add `isAdmin` to `src/policy.ts` and rewrite the three guards *in terms of it* rather than collapsing them together:

```ts
assertAdminA → isAdmin(role)
assertAdminB → isAdmin(role) || isOwner(role)
assertAdminC → !isAdmin(role)          // and rename: it is not an admin assert
```

Same call-site semantics, one literal `"admin"`. `assertAdminC` should be renamed (`isNonAdmin` / `requiresElevation`) — the misleading name is the actual hazard, not the duplication.

## Files that would change

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `src/sanitize.ts` | **new** — the consolidated sanitiser |
| `src/telemetry.ts` | **new** — the consolidated telemetry emitter |
| `src/sanitize-a.ts` | body deleted; re-exports `sanitizeUserInput` as a wrapper over `sanitize`; guard delegates to `isAdmin` |
| `src/sanitize-b.ts` | same, for `sanitizeText`; guard becomes `isAdmin \|\| isOwner` |
| `src/sanitize-c.ts` | same, for `cleanMessage`; guard becomes `!isAdmin`, renamed |
| `src/policy.ts` | adds `isAdmin` (+ `isOwner`); the three `can*` functions delegate to it |
| `src/telemetry-a.ts` | deleted (or shim) |
| `src/telemetry-b.ts` | deleted (or shim) |

Both duplication findings report `blast_radius_importers: 0` — nothing in this fixture imports these modules, so the shims are optional here. In a real repo they're what makes this landable in one commit; drop them in a follow-up once call sites migrate.

## Public API of the consolidated function

```ts
// src/sanitize.ts

export interface SanitizeOptions {
  /** Truncate to this many chars after whitespace collapse. Default 1000. */
  maxLength?: number;
  /** Reject if more than this many runs of 3+ `!`/`?`. Default 5. */
  maxPunctuationRuns?: number;
  /** Lowercase when the uppercase ratio exceeds this. Default 0.9. */
  shoutRatio?: number;
  /** ...but only for strings longer than this. Default 30. */
  shoutMinLength?: number;
}

/**
 * Normalise untrusted text. Returns "" for input judged unusable
 * (empty, markup-leading, escape-sequence-bearing, punctuation-spammy).
 */
export function sanitize(input: string, options?: SanitizeOptions): string;
```

Design notes on that signature:

- **Rejection stays as `""`, not `null` or a thrown error.** All three copies return `""` on every failure path; changing the sentinel is a behaviour change disguised as a cleanup. If callers need to distinguish "empty input" from "rejected input", add a separate `sanitizeWithReason(): { text: string; rejected?: Reason }` alongside — don't reshape the existing return.
- **Options are optional and defaulted to today's constants**, so every existing call site is a drop-in with zero arguments. The parameterisation exists so the next tuning request edits one default instead of three literals.
- **Keep the `null`/`undefined` guard and the `String(...)` coercion** even though the parameter is typed `string`. The type says these are unreachable; the three authors independently disagreed. Removing them is a runtime behaviour change at any un-typechecked boundary — do it separately, if at all.
- **Write the control-char class explicitly as `/[\x00-\x1f]/g`.** In the current source it's raw `\0`–`\037` bytes inside the literal (verified with `od -c`), which renders as an innocuous-looking `[ -]` in most diffs and review tools. That's a genuine agent-risk footgun: an LLM reading the file sees a space-to-hyphen range and will "correct" it.
- **Telemetry stays out of `sanitize`.** `recordSanitiseEvent(originalLength, sanitisedLength, now?)` remains a separate call, so the sanitiser stays pure and testable without stubbing `console.log`.

**One caveat worth stating:** steps 1 and 2 are mechanical and safe. Step 3 is not — `assertAdminC`'s inversion means the "obvious" consolidation is a security regression. If these guards have real call sites in your codebase, verify each one before landing step 3; it's fine to ship 1 and 2 and leave 3 for a reviewed commit of its own.
